articles.title: New wildfire in Southern California explodes in size, burning multiple homes
articles.summary: A fast-moving wildfire in Southern California quickly consumed hundreds of acres and burned multiple homes after sparking in Orange County Friday, county off...
articles.body:
A fast-moving wildfire in Southern California quickly consumed hundreds of acres and burned multiple homes after sparking in Orange County Friday, county officials said.

The Norte Fire began around noon near a neighborhood in the San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano areas and by Friday evening had grown to 570 acres, the Orange County Fire Authority said. It's one of several fires that have broken out since Thursday amid fierce Santa Ana winds affecting Southern California.

"Our actions today will be to continue to attack the fire and work toward getting residents home as soon as it's safe to so do," Orange County Fire Authority Captain Greg Barta said Saturday morning in a video on X .

Topography and weather conditions allowed the fire to grow rapidly, Orange County Division 3 Fire Chief Mark Backoff said in a video posted to social media Friday afternoon.

Six homes have been destroyed or damaged by the fire, and two firefighters suffered "significant" injuries but are stable in area hospitals, fire officials said.

Evacuation orders were issued for multiple areas in San Clemente and San Juan Capistrano, encompassing roughly 4,600 homes and 16,000 people, Orange County Fire Authority Chief TJ McGovern said. Officials asked residents to be patient as they evaluate when it will be safe to return home.

Officials said progress had been made against the fire by the evening but warned conditions remained volatile.

"A majority of the fire has been knocked down. However, we still have some homes that have been impacted here, and as you can see, the wind is still blowing pretty strong up here," Orange County Fire Authority spokesperson Steve Concialdi said.

The fire is now 5% contained as of Saturday morning. Crews' objective is "keeping the fire within its current footprint," McGovern said at a news conference Friday evening.

Aerial footage from CNN affiliate KCBS showed multiple houses burning Friday afternoon.

Resident Robert Morris called the sudden threat to homes "a wake-up call," telling KCBS, "I've lived here since 1995, and this is the first time we've really ever had a fire in this area."

US Rep. Mike Levin, a Democrat whose district includes part of Orange County, said his family had to evacuate their San Juan Capistrano home while he attended an event nearby.

Levin thanked firefighters for preventing greater damage from the fire and said "year-round wildfire season" has become the "new normal" for Southern California.

Orange County sheriff's deputies were going door to door in areas under evacuation order, telling people to leave for their safety, Sgt. Lizbeth Gwisdalla, a spokesperson for the sheriff's department, told CNN.

Ten schools were dismissed early "out of an abundance of caution" and sports and after-school programs were canceled, Capistrano Unified School District announced .

Wind gusts in the area reached 25 mph Friday afternoon and remained elevated into the evening. The Santa Ana winds had eased to gusts of 17 mph by Saturday and are expected to diminish later in the weekend.

"We're going to be here for a number of days," Concialdi said of the ongoing danger, stressing the need to guard against new fires that could erupt from embers blown by the strong Santa Ana winds.

Several fires have broken out since Santa Ana winds began Thursday, forcing evacuations in other areas of Southern California.

In Malibu, more than 7,000 structures were in areas under evacuation orders or warnings on Friday because of the Bryson Fire, which has burned roughly 150 acres and is 52% contained since starting Thursday evening, a Los Angeles County Fire spokesperson told CNN, estimating the number of people under evacuation orders to be in the hundreds.

Crews made "great progress" against the fire overnight, Los Angeles County Fire Chief Anthony Marrone said during a news conference Friday morning.

At least one firefighter had "minor injuries" and was taken to the hospital, he said. The chief did not provide additional details except to say, "They've been on the line all night, so minor injuries are expected."

The fire is still threatening more than 100 structures in the area, but no damages have been reported. "But obviously, if the winds kick up later this afternoon and we were to lose containment of the fire, a larger area could be affected and under threat," the chief said. Over 400 firefighters and more than 75 "ground and aerial resources" are committed to the Bryson Fire, he said.

Another wildfire to the south has burned more than 3,000 acres near the Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton since igniting Thursday afternoon, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection ( Cal Fire ).

The Henderson Fire forced a temporary evacuation order for one area of the base Thursday and the closure of a nearby portion of Interstate 5 in San Diego County, the Marine Corps said in a statement Friday. Smoke affected visibility along both sides of the highway Friday afternoon, the California Highway Patrol said. The fire is 35% contained as of Saturday morning, according to Cal Fire .

The Camp Pendleton Fire Department and Cal Fire continue to actively fight the fire, but it was burning "in a remote section" of the base and there were no active threats to personnel or facilities, the Marine Corps statement Friday said.

The dangerous fire conditions in Southern California have also prompted utility companies to temporarily shut off power for tens of thousands over concerns that equipment could spark fires.

This story has been updated with additional information.

Meteorologist Chris Dolce and CNN's Kate S. Petersen and Isa Mudannayake contributed to this report.

articles.title: In 1968, millions of grey squirrels moved across America in a puzzling wildlife event, and scientists traced a possible clue to the acorn crop of 1967
articles.summary: In the autumn of 1968, reports of eastern grey squirrels moving in unusual numbers across parts of the northeastern United States drew attention to a
articles.body: In the autumn of 1968, reports of eastern grey squirrels moving in unusual numbers across parts of the northeastern United States drew attention to a puzzling wildlife event. The scale of the movement was striking, but the animals had not necessarily begun travelling without reason. Their behaviour may have reflected changes in the food supply that had taken place over several seasons. Acorns, a major source of food for squirrels, vary considerably in abundance from one year to the next. When a good harvest is followed by a poor one, animals that have benefited from plentiful food can suddenly face a very different landscape. The weather in the preceding year may help explain how that imbalance developed.The mystery behind the 1968 eastern grey squirrel migrationEastern grey squirrels (Sciurus carolinensis) depend on a varied diet, but acorns are an important part of their food supply in oak woodland. The number of acorns produced by trees can fluctuate sharply between years. A forest that provides abundant food one autumn may offer much less the next, leaving squirrels with fewer resources just as their numbers may have increased.Some estimates put the number of squirrels involved in the 1968 irruption at 20 million, according to Smithsonian magazine. The unusual movement occurred across parts of the eastern United States, particularly the Appalachian region, where squirrels were reported crossing highways, entering buildings and attempting to swim across lakes and reservoirs.What happened to the acorn crop before the migrationThe study published in Forest Ecology and Management, titled ‘A perfect storm: Weather variability, mast failure, and the 1968 gray squirrel irruption in the eastern US’, investigate the possible causes, scientists examined oak seed production in the Asheville region of North Carolina, an area associated with the 1968 squirrel irruption. Their analysis covered 12 years, from 1962 to 1973, and included five oak species. They compared annual acorn production with temperature and rainfall during the growing season, looking for weather patterns that might help explain why some years produced plentiful crops while others did not.The findings pointed towards a complicated relationship between weather and tree reproduction. Warmer spring and summer conditions were associated with reduced acorn production in several of the species examined. The effects varied according to the type of oak and the stage of development, meaning that a single weather pattern did not affect every tree in the same way.Why the weather in 1967 attracted attentionThe scientists also examined whether the unusual weather associated with the North Carolina records could be detected across the wider northeastern United States. This helped establish whether the conditions affecting local oak production were part of a broader regional pattern rather than something confined to a small area.Some of the weather variables fell towards the extremes of the standard 1961–1990 climate reference period. Summer 1967 temperatures, in particular, stood out as the lowest in that record. This offered a possible clue to the unusual sequence of acorn harvests that preceded the following year's squirrel movement.The relationship was not as simple as saying that one cold summer caused millions of animals to migrate. Tree reproduction responds to conditions over different stages of development, and the effects of weather can carry over from one growing season to another. The study also found evidence that a large crop in one year could be followed by a smaller crop in the next, supporting the idea that trees may need time to replenish resources used during heavy seed production.How a plentiful harvest can contribute to a wildlife irruptionA large crop of acorns does more than feed the squirrels already living in a forest. Abundant food can improve survival and breeding opportunities, allowing more animals to persist in an area. Squirrels also store food for later use, but their caches cannot always compensate for a major shortfall in the following season.If food becomes scarce after a period of abundance, competition increases. Animals may travel further in search of suitable feeding grounds, move into unfamiliar habitats or appear in places where they are not normally seen in large numbers. articles.title: North Korea: What satellite images reveal about Kim Jong Un's summer retreat
articles.summary: Satellite images give clues about how Kim spends his holidays - something far out of reach for most North Koreans.
articles.body:
An 80m (263ft) luxury vessel has been repeatedly spotted in satellite images off North Korea's Wonsan coast from July to mid-October this year.

What stands out is the 50m swimming pool along the deck, with a cluster of waterslides at one end.

After sitting idle for months at a maintenance facility, it relocated in early July to waters off a strip of coastline known as the Kalma Peninsula.

This is close to Wonsan, a seaside resort with a sprawling villa used by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and his family.

It was not the only large vessel on the move. A handful of others were also repeatedly seen near Kim's villa, in satellite images analysed by the BBC.

The vessels are widely believed to be used by Kim and his family. Former North Korean officials, defectors and experts say it would be difficult for anyone unconnected to the regime's leadership to own or freely use vessels of this size.

"In winter, they would keep them at the shipyard. When summer came, they would bring them out and move them to Kim Jong Un's villa or towards Kalma, and use them for swimming and recreation," says Ri Jong Ho.

Ri was once an official at the Workers' Party's Office 39, which is believed to be involved in raising and managing foreign currency for the leadership.

The wealth of those who sit at the top of the secretive North Korean dictatorship is just as hard to pin down as the country's economic figures.

The United Nations and others rely on estimates to classify North Korea as one of the world's poorest countries, with an especially large military budget that funds a sanctioned nuclear programme.

Most North Koreans, according to a 2025 UN report, live under "systematic, widespread and gross human rights violations" with total state control, widespread forced labour, and chronic food shortages that leave an estimated 40% of the population undernourished.

But the regime has long been known to live in luxury.

We don't know the cost of the vessels seen in the satellite imagery, but comparable luxury yachts run from tens of millions to over $100m (£75m). Kim's much smaller, 29-metre Princess yacht was previously estimated to be worth about $7m.

While vessel locations alone cannot definitively establish the family's whereabouts, their movements - which overlap with gaps in Kim's public appearances - point to activities that would otherwise remain out of public view.

Wonsan is where Kim Jong Un spent part of his childhood with his mother, according to biographers and intelligence reports, and one expert told the BBC the city has been associated with the family since his father Kim Jong Il's rule.

A defector who served for 13 years guarding residences used by then leader Kim Jong Il - through the 1990s to the early 2000s - told the BBC the villas around Wonsan were used as a retreat by the elite. He recalls seeing dozens of children and teens waterskiing during summer.

North Korean state media rarely publishes reports about Kim being on holiday, instead framing such visits as official inspections or guidance. But defectors interviewed by the BBC appeared to be aware that the family spent holidays in Wonsan, suggesting that at least some North Koreans knew about it.

North Korean state media also claims Wonsan is home to high-rise hotels, restaurants, shops, sports facilities and water parks, and can accommodate nearly 20,000 visitors.

State media and Russian outlets have published images of small groups of Russian tourists visiting the Wonsan Kalma resort, which opened in July 2025. Although developed to attract foreign visitors, the resort is also open to local tourists.

A South Korean news report, citing an unnamed source, says some locals were offered four-night tour packages for around $100, a substantial sum for most North Koreans. The country's per capita GDP - around $667 in 2024, according to the UN - is a small fraction of South Korea's $36,227.

For the majority of North Koreans, holidays are out of reach. And while a growing middle class does exist, they might not have much time for leisure.

Defectors told the BBC that workers, office employees and cooperative farmers are legally entitled to 14 days of annual leave, but this is rarely followed.

Taking consecutive days off to travel is unusual. People typically take weekend trips or travel during national holidays instead of designated "summer holidays".

Even if leave is granted, travel itself is restricted, with official permission required for people to travel outside their city or county. Moving freely is sometimes as much a luxury as the holiday itself.

The BBC tracked four large vessels around Wonsan, measuring approximately 50m, 55m, 60m and 80m. All four vessels repeatedly appeared around Kim's Wonsan villa this year.

The largest vessel showed the clearest activity, moving from the dock to the waters off the Kalma Peninsula, where it has been since July.

Two of the other vessels - 50m and 55m - were repeatedly seen until the end of August around Tae and Sin islands, close to Wonsan.

Satellite images also showed four smaller boats alongside the 50m vessel.

Satellite imagery expert Jeong Seong-hak said the smaller boats ferried people, fuel and supplies to the larger vessel, adding that small islands like Tae and Sin offered "secluded maritime retreats where privacy can be maintained away from public view".

The 60m vessel was repeatedly seen near Kim's Wonsan villa until as recently as last week.

Though North Korea has never publicly disclosed the vessels' official ownership, BBC's analysis of historical satellite imagery found a large vessel with the same distinctive characteristics in Wonsan in 2002, when Kim Jong Il ruled North Korea.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman, who visited the North in 2013, told The Sun that he had spent much of his seven-day visit with Kim Jong Un around Wonsan, where they went jet-skiing and horse riding.

He also described a 60m vessel they used as a cross between a ferry and a Disney boat. It is not clear if this is the same 60m boat pictured in the above satellite imagery.

To most North Koreans, the life lived by the Kims and others who support the regime would seem not just extravagant but unimaginable. Especially because state propaganda is dedicated to presenting the "supreme leader" as a selfless man who always puts the nation first.

"Kim Jong Un is supposed to be a 'leader of the people'," Ri Jong Ho says, "yet he has four luxury vessels like these while ordinary people are struggling just to get one meal a day."
